1128.title: Zamzam, again
1128.hook: pilgrims drink Zamzam, for whatever purpose it is drunk (Ibn Majah)
1128.howItsDone: Pilgrims drink Zamzam water in the sacred mosque, often making a du'a before drinking, and some bring containers of it home to share with family and friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two rak'ahs behind Ibrahim's station, a stillness after the circling. Your line: where ibrahim stood.

A glass of water, and a question before you drink it: what is this for? On an ordinary day, the question never comes up. Thirst, habit, the meeting running long. But a hadith in the collection of Ibn Majah makes it matter. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported to have said that the water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for. Not just thirst. Whatever the drinker brings to it. You met this well back on day forty. Today it comes back, in the middle of the pilgrimage, with a new job.
screen: `A GLASS OF WATER.` → `WHAT IS THIS FOR?` → `FOR WHATEVER IT IS DRUNK FOR.`

segments.voice: First, where the water comes from. Zamzam is a well inside the sacred mosque in Mecca, close to the Ka'ba. In a long report in Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Abbas tells how it first appeared: a mother alone in a dry valley with her baby, searching, and water breaking out of the ground. Her search is tomorrow's story. Second, the Prophet at the well. Jabir's account of the pilgrimage, in Sahih Muslim, has him coming to the people of his own clan as they drew water at Zamzam and gave it out. They handed him a bucket, and he drank. Ibn Abbas adds, in Bukhari, that he was the one who gave the Prophet Zamzam, and that the Prophet drank it standing. A man, a bucket, a crowd, a drink. Third, the hadith from Ibn Majah. Some pilgrims take it literally. They stand by the taps and fountains, and before they drink, or while they drink, they ask for something. Healing for someone at home. Knowledge. Forgiveness. A child. Some carry bottles of it home for the people who couldn't come. Scholars have discussed the grading of this hadith, and readers take it in different ways; the habit it has formed is easy to see at the fountains. Fourth, what changes. Nothing about the glass is different. The water is still water. What changes is that the drinker stops, names a purpose, and turns a reflex into a request.
screen: `A WELL NEAR THE KA'BA.` · `A BUCKET, AND HE DRANK.` · `FOR WHATEVER IT IS DRUNK FOR.` · `A REFLEX TURNED INTO A REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Hold a glass of ordinary water, if you have one, and before you drink, name one thing you hope for, for yourself or for someone else, plainly and quietly. If you pray, make it a du'a in your own words and say bismillah; if not, just name the hope. Then drink slowly.
Zamzam. The well beside the Ka'ba, whose water, the hadith says, is for whatever it is drunk for. Today's word.
Your line: drink with intention. The water stays the same; the drinker changes. Until tomorrow.

1129.title: Safa and Marwa
1129.hook: walking seven times between the hills, as Hajar ran
1129.howItsDone: After tawaf, pilgrims perform sa'y: seven lengths between Safa and Marwa, starting at Safa and ending at Marwa, now inside a long gallery of the sacred mosque, with men hurrying between the green markers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zamzam, the water drunk for whatever it's drunk for. Your line: drink with intention.

A woman stands on top of a small rocky hill, shading her eyes, looking out over an empty valley. Her water is gone. Her baby is crying below. She sees nobody. So she comes down, crosses the low ground, running where the valley dips, and climbs the hill on the other side. She looks again. Nobody. Back she goes. The woman is Hajar, and Ibn Abbas tells her story in Sahih al-Bukhari. Today, the walk pilgrims make in her footsteps.
screen: `A WOMAN ON A HILL.` → `HER WATER IS GONE.` → `SHE RUNS TO THE OTHER HILL.`

segments.voice: First, her story, which you first met back on day thirty-nine. In Ibn Abbas's telling, Ibrahim leaves Hajar and their baby, Ismail, in the valley with a little food and water. She follows him and asks: has Allah commanded you to do this? He says yes. And she answers: then He will not abandon us. When the water runs out, she climbs Safa, then Marwa, back and forth, seven times, looking for help. At the end she hears a sound, and the water of yesterday's well breaks out of the ground. Second, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ's comment, kept in the same report: that is why people walk between the two. Her searching became their rite. Third, what the Qur'an says. In Pickthall's translation of surah two: "Lo! (the mountains) As-Safa and Al-Marwah are among the indications of Allah." Jabir, in Sahih Muslim, says that when the Prophet came near Safa, he recited that verse and said, I begin with what Allah began with. So the walk starts at Safa, as the verse does. Fourth, the walk today. The two hills are inside the mosque now, joined by a long covered corridor. Pilgrims walk seven lengths in all, and in the low stretch between, marked out for them, the men hurry, the way she ran where the valley dipped. Look at who sets the pace. Not a prophet, not a king. A mother, alone, worried, doing everything she could while she trusted that she wouldn't be abandoned. The pilgrims, whoever they are at home, walk behind her.
screen: `THEN HE WILL NOT ABANDON US.` · `HER SEARCH BECAME THEIR RITE.` · `SAFA AND MARWA, SIGNS OF ALLAH.` · `THE PILGRIMS WALK BEHIND HER.`

segments.voice: Choose two points, a door and a window, a wall and a chair, and walk between them seven times, counting as you go, quickening your step a little on one stretch in the middle, the way she ran. If you pray, make du'a as you walk; if not, hold in mind someone who is searching for something right now.
Sa'y. The walk between Safa and Marwa, seven lengths, in Hajar's footsteps. Today's word.
Your line: in her footsteps. She did all she could, and trusted the rest. On to Mina tomorrow.

1130.title: The eighth: Mina
1130.hook: pilgrims go to Mina, a city of tents
1130.howItsDone: On the eighth of Dhul-Hijjah, pilgrims enter ihram for Hajj if they are not already in it and go to Mina, where they pray the day's prayers, shortening those of four units, and spend the night before moving on to Arafah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sa'y, seven lengths between Safa and Marwa in Hajar's footsteps. Your line: in her footsteps.

On the eighth day, where did the Prophet pray the noon prayer? Abd al-Aziz ibn Rufay wanted a straight answer, so he asked Anas ibn Malik, a companion of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: tell me something you remember. Anas answered: at Mina. The exchange is in Sahih al-Bukhari, and it's how the days of Hajj itself begin. Not at the Ka'ba. Outside the city, in a valley of tents. Today, the eighth.
screen: `WHERE DID HE PRAY AT NOON?` → `AT MINA.` → `A VALLEY OF TENTS.`

segments.voice: First, the date. The circling and the walking can be done at other times of year too. Hajj proper has its own days in the month of Dhul-Hijjah, and in Jabir's account they begin on the eighth, the day of tarwiyah. Pilgrims who have come out of ihram enter it again, and the crowd moves out of Mecca to Mina. Second, what the Prophet did there. Jabir's account in Sahih Muslim says that on that day they set out for Mina, and the Prophet prayed there the noon, afternoon, sunset, evening and dawn prayers. Then he waited a little until the sun had risen, and went on. That's the whole of the eighth: travel, five prayers, one night, and waiting. No great ritual. A pause before Arafah. Third, the place now. Mina today is a valley filled with row after row of tents, white and fireproof, set up for the days of Hajj and almost empty the rest of the year. People from far and wide sleep side by side on thin mattresses, share food, queue for the washrooms, and pray together on carpets laid over the ground. The surgeon in white cloth from a week ago now shares a tent with strangers. Fourth, the end of Anas's answer. He closed with a line: do as your leaders do. Pilgrims follow the group, move when it moves, rest when it rests. The Qur'an, in surah two, speaks of the days spent here later in the Hajj; in Pickthall's words: "Remember Allah through the appointed days." A city of tents is made for exactly that: not much to do, and plenty of time to remember.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY OF HAJJ PROPER.` · `FIVE PRAYERS AND ONE NIGHT.` · `STRANGERS SIDE BY SIDE.` · `DO AS YOUR LEADERS DO.`

segments.voice: Sit somewhere snug, a corner of a room, the edge of a bed, a parked car, with nothing to do, and notice how close the walls are and how little you need. If you pray, use the time for remembrance, a few words of praise you know, said slowly; if not, stay with the breath and the smallness of the space.
The eighth. The eighth of Dhul-Hijjah, when pilgrims go out to Mina, pray, and spend the night in tents. Today's word.
Your line: a city of tents. Strangers side by side, with time to remember. Same time tomorrow.

1131.title: The ninth: Arafah
1131.hook: standing on the plain from noon to sunset: Hajj is Arafah (Tirmidhi)
1131.howItsDone: On the ninth of Dhul-Hijjah, pilgrims go from Mina to the plain of Arafah, pray the noon and afternoon prayers together, and spend the afternoon until sunset in du'a, recitation and remembrance before moving on to Muzdalifah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eighth, five prayers and a night in the tents at Mina. Your line: a city of tents.

A group of travelers arrives at the plain of Arafah and finds the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ there. They have one question: what is the Hajj? A man is sent to call out his answer to the crowd, and it's short. The Hajj is Arafah. The report, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mar, is in the collection of Tirmidhi. The cloths, the circling, the walking, the tents: all of it leads to this one day. Today, the ninth.
screen: `TRAVELERS WITH ONE QUESTION.` → `WHAT IS THE HAJJ?` → `THE HAJJ IS ARAFAH.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Wuquf means standing, and it's the name for being present on the plain of Arafah on the ninth day. You met this day from home back on day one hundred twenty-eight; today, the plain itself. Tirmidhi's report goes on: whoever reaches Arafah before dawn after that night has caught the Hajj. Miss it, and in the teaching of the scholars the Hajj itself is missed, whatever else was done. Second, what the Prophet did. Jabir's account in Sahih Muslim says he left Mina after sunrise, and when the sun passed its height, he addressed the people; then the noon and afternoon prayers were prayed together. Then he rode to the place of standing, faced the qiblah, and stayed there, still on his camel, until the sun had set. Noon to sunset: that's the shape of the day. Third, what standing means. It doesn't require being on your feet. Pilgrims sit under umbrellas, stand by the roadside, rest in tents, lift their hands, read the Qur'an, cry, say nothing at all. The rite is being there, turned toward God, for those hours. Fourth, why this day. Aisha reports, in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet saying that there is no day on which Allah sets free more servants from the Fire than the day of Arafah. So the plain fills with people asking, for themselves, for their parents, for names written on scraps of paper by people at home. At sunset the whole crowd moves at once. Surah two gives the instruction for that moment, in Pickthall's words: "But, when ye press on in the multitude from 'Arafat, remember Allah by the sacred monument." That's where tomorrow begins.
screen: `WUQUF: STANDING, BEING THERE.` · `FROM NOON TO SUNSET.` · `ON YOUR FEET OR NOT.` · `NO DAY FREES MORE SERVANTS.`

segments.voice: Stand, or sit if standing is hard, and turn your palms up; pilgrims give a whole afternoon to this, and a few minutes is a real start. If you pray, ask in your own words for yourself and then for someone else by name; if not, hold in mind what you most hope for, and one person you hope it for too.
Wuquf. Standing on the plain of Arafah, from noon to sunset on the ninth, the heart of the Hajj. Today's word.
Your line: hajj is arafah. One afternoon of being there is the heart of it all. See you at Muzdalifah.

1132.title: The night at Muzdalifah
1132.hook: a night under the sky and pebbles gathered
1132.howItsDone: After sunset on the day of Arafah, pilgrims travel to Muzdalifah, pray maghrib and isha together, spend the night on open ground, and gather pebbles for the stoning; the elderly and weak may move on during the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wuquf, standing on the plain of Arafah from noon to sunset. Your line: hajj is arafah.

The sun is down over Arafah, and nobody has prayed maghrib, the sunset prayer. A whole crowd is moving off the plain with it still waiting. On the road, Usama ibn Zayd, riding behind the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, reminds him: the prayer, Messenger of God. The answer comes back: the prayer is ahead of you. Ahead, in the dark, is a stretch of open ground between Arafah and Mina. Tonight the pilgrims sleep there, under the sky. Today, the night at Muzdalifah.
screen: `MAGHRIB HASN'T BEEN PRAYED.` → `THE PRAYER IS AHEAD OF YOU.` → `OPEN GROUND, UNDER THE SKY.`

segments.voice: The step-by-step telling of this night comes from Jabir ibn Abdullah, whose account of the Prophet's Hajj is kept in Sahih Muslim. First, the prayers. When they reach Muzdalifah, he prays maghrib and isha together, with one call to prayer, and nothing prayed between them. Second, the sleep. Then, Jabir says, he lay down until dawn. That's the whole report of the night. After a day of standing in du'a, the account describes rest. Some scholars point out what isn't there: no long night vigil is described, and they take the sleep itself as part of what the Prophet did. Third, the mercy. Not everyone stays until dawn. Ibn Abbas reports that he was among the weaker members of the Prophet's household who were sent on ahead during the night. Jurists draw on that permission for the elderly, the unwell, and those caring for them. Fourth, the morning. At dawn he prays fajr, then goes to the place the Qur'an calls the sacred monument, al-Mash'ar al-Haram, where Surah Al-Baqarah tells the pilgrims to remember God as He has guided them. He faces the qiblah, praises God, and stays until the sky is bright, then moves on before the sun comes up. And the pebbles: pilgrims often pick up small stones here for the next morning's rite, though some schools allow gathering them elsewhere too. A night on the ground, a pocket of pebbles, and nothing between the sleeper and the sky.
screen: `TWO PRAYERS, JOINED.` · `HE LAY DOWN UNTIL DAWN.` · `THE WEAK SENT AHEAD.` · `DAWN AT THE SACRED MONUMENT.` · then, large: `THE PRAYER IS AHEAD OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Lie down on the floor, or sit low, close to the ground, and feel what's holding you up; for now nothing is asked of you except to be still, the way the pilgrims lie on that open ground. If you pray, say a quiet alhamdulillah for the day that's ending; if not, name one thing today asked of you, and set it down.
The night at Muzdalifah. The night after Arafah: two prayers joined, sleep on open ground, remembrance at dawn, and pebbles gathered for the morning. Today's word.
Your line: a night under the sky. After the long standing, rest is part of the journey too. Sleep well.

1133.title: The stoning
1133.hook: pebbles thrown at pillars where Ibrahim rejected Shaytan's whispers
1133.howItsDone: On the day of sacrifice pilgrims throw small pebbles at the pillar called Jamrat al-Aqabah at Mina, saying Allahu akbar with each, and on the following days they stone all the pillars.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the night at Muzdalifah, two prayers joined and sleep on open ground. Your line: a night under the sky.

Small stones. That's what the morning after Muzdalifah comes down to. On the day of sacrifice, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reaches a pillar in the valley at Mina and throws pebbles at it, one at a time. On the road before, he asks Ibn Abbas to pick some up for him. Ibn Abbas brings back little ones, the kind you could flick between a finger and a thumb. The Prophet shakes them in his hand and says: like these. Not rocks. Nothing bigger to make a point. Today's word is the place those small stones are thrown.
screen: `SMALL STONES.` → `PICK SOME UP FOR ME.` → `LIKE THESE.`

segments.voice: Jamarat: the pillars of Mina, and the rite of stoning them. Start with what the Prophet did. In Jabir's account in Sahih Muslim, he comes to the jamrah, throws seven small pebbles, and says Allahu akbar with each one. A throw, and God is greater. Next, the size, and a warning. In the report from Ibn Abbas in al-Nasa'i, after like these, the Prophet adds: beware of going to extremes in religion, because extremes destroyed those who came before. The pebbles are small on purpose. The rite doesn't need anger to work. Then, the story people tell. A report attributed to Ibn Abbas says that at these spots Shaytan appeared to Ibrahim, trying to turn him from what God had asked, and Ibrahim drove him off with stones. It isn't in the Qur'an; it's a report kept in the hadith books, and the tradition remembers the stoning through it. Last, what the rite is for. Aisha is reported, in Sunan Abi Dawud, to have said that the circling of the House, the walk between Safa and Marwa, and the stoning were set up for the remembrance of God. So the target isn't really the pillar. The Qur'an's closing surah names the enemy: "the sneaking whisperer, Who whispereth in the hearts of mankind." You met that whisper back on day twenty-six. It doesn't shout. It suggests. And the answer the rite rehearses is just as quiet: a small stone, a clear refusal, God is greater. Pilgrims do it again in the days that follow. A whisper comes back, so the refusal comes back too.
screen: `SEVEN PEBBLES, A TAKBIR EACH.` · `SMALL, ON PURPOSE.` · `IBRAHIM DROVE HIM OFF.` · `SET UP FOR REMEMBRANCE.` · then, large: `THE SNEAKING WHISPERER.`

segments.voice: Let one familiar thought come up, the quiet one that nudges you toward something you'd rather not do, and don't fight it; just name it, plainly, as a whisper. If you pray, say a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim, the words Muslims use to seek refuge from Shaytan; if not, picture a small stone in your hand, and set the thought down with it.
Jamarat. The pillars at Mina where pilgrims throw small pebbles, a takbir with each, remembering Ibrahim's refusal. Today's word.

1134.title: The sacrifice
1134.hook: an animal is sacrificed, and the meat shared
1134.howItsDone: Pilgrims offer an animal at Mina after the stoning, and Muslims at home who are able offer one at Eid al-Adha; the meat is eaten by the household and shared with friends and with people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the jamarat, small stones and a takbir with each. Your line: reject the whisper.

A rule about leftovers, and then a change to it. One Eid in Medina, Aisha reports, a group of poor families arrived from the desert. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told the people: keep the meat of your sacrifice for three days, and give away the rest. Later, people came to him unsure. Were they still bound by it? His answer: I only forbade it because of the families who had come. Now eat, store, and give. The rule had been shaped around hungry guests. Today, the sacrifice.
screen: `A RULE ABOUT LEFTOVERS.` → `FAMILIES ARRIVE HUNGRY.` → `NOW EAT, STORE, AND GIVE.`

segments.voice: Back at Mina, after the stoning, Jabir's account in Sahih Muslim says the Prophet went to the place of sacrifice and offered animals with his own hand. Then a piece from each was cooked, and he ate of the meat and drank of the broth. That's the first thing to notice: the one who offered it sat down and ate. The sacrifice becomes a meal. Second, who else eats. Surah Al-Hajj tells those who sacrifice to eat of it and to feed two kinds of people: the one who is content and doesn't ask, and the one who does ask. The quiet poor, and the poor who knock. Third, the line that turns the whole act around. The same surah says: "Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." The meat stays here, on plates. What goes up is something you can't weigh. Fourth, Aisha's story from the hook, in Sahih Muslim: a rule about storing meat, set because hungry families had come, and loosened when they hadn't. The sacrifice keeps looking at who is at the door. And it isn't only for pilgrims. At Eid al-Adha, Muslims at home who are able offer an animal too, and remember Ibrahim, whose story of a ransomed son is told in Surah As-Saffat. So the same day, at Mina and far from it, there's blood, then a fire, then a pot, then a knock, then a plate passed across a table.
screen: `HE ATE OF THE MEAT.` · `THE CONTENT AND THE ONE WHO ASKS.` · `THE DEVOTION REACHES HIM.` · `A RULE SHAPED BY HUNGRY GUESTS.` · then, large: `THEIR FLESH AND THEIR BLOOD REACH NOT ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Think of the food you'll eat in the next day or two, and of one person who could share some of it: someone who'd never ask, a neighbor, an older relative, a coworker eating alone, or someone who would ask if they knew they could. Picture handing them the plate. If you pray, thank God for the food first; if not, just hold the picture.
The sacrifice. An animal offered in God's name on the day of sacrifice, its meat eaten and shared, and only the devotion reaching God. Today's word.
Your line: shared meat. The week ran from Zamzam, through Safa and Marwa, Mina, Arafah and Muzdalifah, to the stones and the sacrifice. Eat well, and see you tomorrow.
